title: JS: the language core (topics 01-14)
_note: rv2 S2 (PLAN §2.2 fund-js-core row). Scope = Fundamentals JS topic gates 01-14. Sources = the topic gate plus its first drill; siblings = the topic's bug-hunt drill and content/fundamentals/related.json drills. Topics 03 and 08 carry no idea of their own (not on the binding list). Server-local side file, never stamped.

ideas.idea: Compare with === and convert on purpose (Number(), String()); pick ?? for defaults when 0, '' or false are valid values, because || replaces every falsy value.
ideas.why: Loose equality and || defaults silently turn a real 0 or empty string into something else: a quantity of zero becomes the default, a form field compares equal to the wrong value.
ideas.prompt: A settings form sends { volume: 0 }. The code does `const volume = input.volume || 50`. The user complains their mute setting never sticks. Explain the bug and the fix.
ideas.answer: || falls back on any falsy value, and 0 is falsy, so a deliberate 0 becomes 50. Use `input.volume ?? 50`: nullish coalescing only falls back on null or undefined. When the value arrives as a string from a form, convert it explicitly with Number() and check for NaN before using it.

ideas.idea: A closure keeps a live reference to the variable, not a copy of its value at creation time; let in a loop gives each iteration its own binding.
ideas.why: Callbacks created in a loop or before a reassignment read the variable's latest value, so every handler sees the same final index or a changed setting.
ideas.prompt: Inside `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0)` the output is 3, 3, 3. A junior says 'closures copy i'. Correct them and give two fixes.
ideas.answer: Closures do not copy: all three callbacks share the one function-scoped var i, and by the time they run the loop has made it 3. Declare the loop variable with let, which creates a fresh binding per iteration, or pass the current value in as an argument so each callback closes over its own variable.

ideas.idea: The receiver of a method call is decided at the call, not where the method was written; an arrow borrows the receiver of the code around it.
ideas.why: Passing a method as a callback detaches it from its object, so this becomes undefined in strict code and the method throws or writes to the wrong place.
ideas.prompt: `button.addEventListener('click', counter.increment)` throws 'cannot read properties of undefined' inside increment, which uses this.count. Why, and what are your options?
ideas.answer: The listener calls the bare function, not counter.increment(), so this is not counter. Bind it (counter.increment.bind(counter)), wrap it in an arrow that calls counter.increment(), or define increment as an arrow class field so it captures the instance. The call site, not the definition, decides what this is.

ideas.idea: A property lookup walks the prototype chain until it finds the name; class syntax builds the same chain, with methods on the prototype shared by every instance.
ideas.why: Without the chain you cannot explain why a method exists on an object you never assigned it to, why a merge can pollute every object, or what class really adds.
ideas.prompt: A deep-merge helper copies keys from a JSON payload into a config object. An attacker sends a key called '__proto__'. After the merge, unrelated objects suddenly have an isAdmin property. Explain the mechanism.
ideas.answer: Writing through '__proto__' reaches the shared Object.prototype, and every plain object finds isAdmin there because lookups walk up the chain when a property is missing. A safe merge skips '__proto__', 'constructor' and 'prototype', only copies own keys, or builds results with Object.create(null).

ideas.idea: Know which array methods change the array they are called on and which hand back a fresh copy, and use a copying one when the caller still needs the original.
ideas.why: Sorting or splicing an array that came from props, state or a cache changes it for every other reader, causing bugs far from the line that did it.
ideas.prompt: A React component renders `props.items.sort(byPrice)` and the parent's list order changes as well, sometimes on every render. What happened, and what do you write instead?
ideas.answer: sort reorders the array in place and returns that same array, so the component mutated its parent's data. Copy first, `[...props.items].sort(byPrice)`, or use `props.items.toSorted(byPrice)`, which returns a new sorted array. The same care applies to splice and reverse.

ideas.idea: Use Map and Set for keyed collections and membership; JSON keeps only plain data, so undefined, functions, Map, Set and Date types do not survive a round trip.
ideas.why: Plain objects as dictionaries collide with inherited keys, and serialising rich types through JSON quietly loses data or changes types on the way back.
ideas.prompt: A cache stores `new Map([[userId, { lastSeen: new Date(), tags: new Set(['a']) }]])` in localStorage with JSON.stringify and reads it back. What comes back, and how do you fix it?
ideas.answer: JSON.stringify writes a Map and a Set as {}, and a Date as an ISO string, so you get an empty object and, at best, strings instead of dates. Convert on purpose: entries arrays for the Map and Set, explicit date strings, then rebuild the types when reading, or use a replacer and reviver pair.

ideas.idea: Throw Error instances, subclass them for errors callers must tell apart, and wrap with { cause } to keep the original; never swallow an error silently.
ideas.why: Thrown strings lose the stack, an empty catch hides real failures, and a rewrapped error without cause erases the clue you need at 3 a.m.
ideas.prompt: A repository catches a database failure and throws new Error('could not load user'). On-call cannot tell whether it was a timeout or a bad query. What should the code have done?
ideas.answer: Keep the original as the cause: `throw new UserLoadError('could not load user', { cause: err })`, with a subclass the API layer can map to the right status. Log the chain once at the boundary. Catch only what you can handle, and rethrow anything else instead of returning a default.

ideas.idea: ES modules are linked statically and imports are live bindings to the exporter's variable; CommonJS require returns a copy of exports as they are when it runs.
ideas.why: Mixing the two explains 'my import is stale' and circular-import undefined values, and why imports cannot be inside an if while require can.
ideas.prompt: Module A exports `let count = 0` and a function that increments it. Module B imports count and calls the function, then logs count. What does B see under ESM, and what under CommonJS when A assigns its exports object and B destructures it?
ideas.answer: Under ESM B sees 1: the import is a live view of A's variable. Under CommonJS B destructured a copy of the value at require time, so it still sees 0 unless it reads a property of the shared exports object after the call. ESM imports are also hoisted and static; require runs when reached.

ideas.idea: After each task, the event loop drains all microtasks (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) before the next macrotask such as a timer or I/O callback runs.
ideas.why: Ordering bugs and starved timers come from assuming setTimeout(fn, 0) runs before a resolved promise's callback, or from microtasks that keep queueing more.
ideas.prompt: Predict the order: `setTimeout(() => log('timeout'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => log('then')); log('sync')`. Then explain why a recursive promise chain can make a timeout never fire.
ideas.answer: sync, then, timeout. Synchronous code runs first, then the microtask queue is emptied, then the timer's macrotask runs. Because the whole microtask queue drains before any macrotask, a chain that keeps queueing new promise callbacks never lets the timer, or I/O, run.

ideas.idea: await inside a loop runs the calls one after another; Promise.all runs them together but rejects on the first failure, while allSettled waits for every result.
ideas.why: Sequential awaits make a page ten times slower than needed, and Promise.all hides which of the other calls succeeded when one fails.
ideas.prompt: A report loads 20 customer records with `for (const id of ids) rows.push(await fetchCustomer(id))`. It takes 4 seconds. One record often fails and the whole report breaks. Redesign it.
ideas.answer: Start the calls together instead of one per loop turn, with a concurrency limit if the API needs it. Use Promise.allSettled so a single failure does not discard the other results: render what succeeded and list the failed ids. Promise.all suits only the case where one failure should abort everything.

ideas.idea: Iterators and generators are lazy: each value is produced only when the consumer asks for it, so a pipeline can stop early or walk an endless source.
ideas.why: Building full arrays at every step wastes memory on large inputs and cannot express an infinite or streamed sequence.
ideas.prompt: You need the first 10 lines of a 2 GB log that match a pattern. A colleague reads all lines into an array, filters, then slices. Describe a lazy version and why it is better.
ideas.answer: Write generators: one yields lines as they are read, a second yields only the matches, and the consumer stops after ten. Nothing is computed past the tenth match, memory stays at one chunk, and breaking out of the for...of loop calls return() so the reader can close the file.
